targets.approach: Same general Snowy Lakes basecamp approach as the standard route (PCT from Rainy Pass), continuing to the base of the northeast side of the peak; expect to find your own way from there.
targets.name: Northeast Arête
South Ridge (North Peak)
targets.parent: Hwy 20 and North Cascades National Park

targets.name: North Ridge (South Peak)
targets.parent: Hwy 20 and North Cascades National Park

targets.approach: From the Lightning Creek trailhead on Ross Lake, the first-ascent party hiked east past Willow Lake, then left the trail to bushwhack through timber and avalanche debris, crossed a ravine, and climbed steep dirt and brush to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. They reached meadows near 5,000 ft and bypassed cliff bands to a saddle at about 6,200 ft below the buttress — roughly six hours from the trailhead — where they bivouacked.
targets.name: Southeast Buttress (South Peak)
targets.parent: Hwy 20 and North Cascades National Park

targets.approach: From the Hozomeen Lake/Willow Lake trailhead at Hozomeen Campground (roughly 1,650-1,720 ft), a maintained trail runs 1.5 to several miles before climbers leave it near Hozomeen Lake's outlet, cross Hozomeen Creek, and push east through heavy deadfall and devil's club into the peak's west basin. This gains a rib/gully system leading to a high camp or bivy around 4,900-5,000 ft, and on to a saddle reported at roughly 6,800 ft below the final pitches.
targets.descent: Parties describe descending the same line: downclimbing and rappelling the technical sections and retracing the gully/rib system back to the basin.
targets.name: Southwest Route (South Peak)
targets.parent: Hwy 20 and North Cascades National Park

targets.name: Southwest Buttress (North Peak)
targets.parent: Hwy 20 and North Cascades National Park

targets.approach: From Lake Ingalls, head toward the ridge on climbers' right of the large couloir on the peak's east side; easy ledges lead to the base of the ridge.
targets.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the East Peak Southwest Face route (3 rap stations) back down to the North-East Peak notch, then reverse the approach terrain to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass.
targets.name: East Peak (Northeast Ridge to East Face)
Northeast Shoulder
siblings: wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route = West Ridge / North Ridge via Chetwoot Lake

targets.name: South Route
siblings: wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route = West Ridge / North Ridge via Chetwoot Lake

wa_classic_route_3.approach: Start from the Reflection Lake pullout on Stevens Canyon Road (open roughly Memorial Day through mid-October) or, when the road is gated by snow, from the Narada Falls pullout — from Narada Falls a short, steep ~200 ft climb through open timber gets you up to Stevens Canyon Road. From either start, walk the road roughly half a mile to the point where it bends sharply and begins heading east; leave the pavement here and drop south through sparse, open forest toward Tatoosh Creek, losing a couple hundred feet to reach it around 4,500 ft. Cross the creek (a rock-hop most of the season, more involved during peak snowmelt) and angle up onto a broad talus slope — about 250 vertical feet — that runs down to the creek (snow-covered in spring, boulder-hopping by mid/late summer). At the top of the talus, continue up through trees staying right of a short cliff band (the timber here is brushy and it's easy to drift toward the cliff if you're not paying attention). Roughly 700 ft above the creek crossing (~5,200 ft) you break out of the trees onto open slopes and continue up to the broad 5,440 ft saddle between Lane Peak and Denman Peak. From the saddle, turn right (west) and climb moderate o
wa_classic_route_3.descent_text: This is mostly a downclimb; the sturdy tree in the gully allows an optional rappel over the loosest section. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the summit scramble and the southeast-face gully back to the 5,440 ft Lane–Denman saddle, then drop east back through the timber (staying right of the cliff band on the way down, mirroring the ascent line) to the top of the talus slope. Descend the talus to Tatoosh Creek, re-cross, and climb back up to Stevens Canyon Road, then walk back to the Narada Falls or Reflection Lake pullout. Watch for loose rock and inconsistent glissade conditions in the gully (plunge-stepping is fine on consolidated snow but the gully holds loose rock once it melts out), and take care not to cliff yourself out in the timber band by drifting off the ascent line.
wa_classic_route_3.name: Classic Route

wa_east_ridge_9.approach: Same trailhead and initial trail as the South Ridge: Esmeralda Basin/Ingalls Lake Trailhead, Ingalls Way Trail (#1390), ~3 miles to Ingalls Pass, then traverse to Lake Ingalls (~4-4.5 miles, ~2,500 ft gain) as described for the South Ridge. From the lake, the East Ridge approach diverges: hike around the lake's left (west/north) side and cross a band of slabs to reach a large talus gully that runs fairly directly up to the saddle/notch separating the east ridge of North Ingalls Peak from East Ingalls Peak (a boot path is intermittently visible in the talus). This gully-and-saddle approach is steeper and looser than the South Ridge's slab approach, so expect more class 2-3 scree/talus travel with some loose rock hazard, especially with parties above. At the saddle, many climbers stash approach gear (extra shoes, poles) in a small cave/nook just below the notch. The route itself starts roughly 30 feet below the saddle on its east side, marked by slings on the first anchor. As with the South Ridge, water is available at Lake Ingalls but not beyond it, and the open talus slopes carry afternoon-storm and loose-rock exposure - climb early and be alert for parties above dislodging rock in
wa_east_ridge_9.descent_text: Do not rappel the East Ridge itself: the ridgeline lacks good rappel anchors and is loose and exposed in a way that makes retracing it dangerous. Instead, from the summit, scramble back to the North-South ridge crest and use the South Ridge rappel line from its three-bolt summit anchor. On a single 60 m rope it is four rappels, one per pitch: a short one to the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 3; one toward the big ledge with a slung boulder above pitch 2, which comes up about 15 ft short so you downclimb the last bit; one down pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1; and one to the base. With two 60 m ropes it is three, going straight from the pitch-2 ledge to the base. Do not skip from the summit straight to the top of pitch 2 in one long rappel: a crack just below the top anchor is known for jamming ropes. Anchors are a mix of fixed bolts and natural slung-boulder anchors reinforced with webbing, so carry spare tat. From the base, downclimb the class 3-4 gully back to the notch and retrace the approach across the slabs to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass to the trailhead.
wa_east_ridge_9.name: East Ridge

wa_golden_horn_east_face.approach: From a camp at Snowy Lakes (reached either on the PCT from Rainy Pass or, as the first-ascent party did, off-trail up Swamp Creek), the first-ascent party scrambled the ridge and traversed a scree field on the mountain's southwest side, then descended to the base of the east face before roping up.
wa_golden_horn_east_face.descent_text: The snow couloir on Golden Horn's east side belongs to the approach: from the ridge above Snowy Lakes it drops to the foot of the east face and is easy going with crampons and an axe. It is not the way off the route, so work out the descent from the top before committing to the face.
wa_golden_horn_east_face.name: East Face

wa_golden_horn_north_face.approach: The standard access to Golden Horn's north side starts from the Rainy Pass PCT North trailhead on Hwy 20, following the PCT north over Cutthroat and Granite Passes and up the small, unsigned spur to Snowy Lakes (~6,700 ft); a rougher, off-trail alternative bushwhacks up Swamp Creek from a highway pullout about 3 miles before Rainy Pass. From Snowy Lakes, travel northwest toward Golden Horn's basin to access the north aspect; this is the general basin-access line reported by parties, not pitch-by-pitch beta for the original 1958 North Face route.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.descent_text: Descend the Southwest Route: a short rappel of about 40 ft off the summit block regains the ridge, then class 2-3 scree and talus on the southwest side lead back down to Snowy Lakes. From camp, retrace the PCT over Granite and Cutthroat Passes to Rainy Pass.
wa_golden_horn_north_face.name: North Face

wa_golden_horn_southwest_route.approach: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Rainy Pass (4,880 ft) near milepost 158, about 35 miles west of Winthrop or 51 miles east of Marblemount. Park at the Rainy Pass North (PCT) trailhead. Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail through forest and switchbacks to Cutthroat Pass (~6,800 ft), continue past Granite Pass (~6.25 miles in, where snowfields can linger into August) and along a cliff-cut trail toward Methow Pass. About a mile before Methow Pass, a small, unsigned spur trail switchbacks up to Lower and then Upper Snowy Lake (~6,700–7,000 ft) — roughly 10–11 miles and 2,700 ft of gain one-way from the trailhead. Good campsites sit in the meadow near the lakes.
wa_golden_horn_southwest_route.descent_text: From the summit, most parties make a single short rappel (roughly 40 ft; a 30m rope is plenty) off the summit block to regain the ridge, then downclimb/scramble class 2–3 scree and talus back toward Snowy Lakes — plunge-stepping the loose scree speeds this considerably. From camp, retrace the PCT approach back over Granite and Cutthroat Passes to Rainy Pass.
wa_golden_horn_southwest_route.name: Southwest Route

wa_hibox_mountain_standard.approach: Start at the Rachel Lake Trailhead (Trail #1313, elev. ~2,800 ft) at the end of Box Canyon Road/FR-4930. Follow the Rachel Lake Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the Box Canyon Creek drainage — the grade is easy and well-graded here, mostly Class 1 hiking. At roughly 2–2.2 miles and about 450–500 ft of gain (~3,300 ft elevation), the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing where Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast; this clearing is the key landmark. Just past it (some parties note it's after the second such clearing), watch on the right/climber's-right side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path (the 'Hibox climbers' path') leaving the maintained trail and heading northeast/uphill into the forest — it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. From here the character changes completely: the bootpath climbs steeply (mostly Class 2, with fallen timber to step over) before breaking out of the trees near a band of cliffs around 5,300 ft. Stay right of this first rock band, then work left around a rock outcrop, continuing through patchy timber to a second, higher cliff band; a gully on the right provides pass
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than glissading the scree, which is loose and eroded. From the summit, downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the south side of the summit block (good rock, low exposure, easy Class 3 moves), then pick your way back down through the loose talus/scree field to the sloping meadow. Some parties descend via a slightly different line on the east side of the summit block/east ridge before rejoining the ascent boot path lower down — functionally the same route, just avoid cutting new paths through the scree to limit erosion. Continue down through the two cliff bands (reversing right/left as on the way up) and back into the timber, staying alert for the boot path's exit point onto the maintained Rachel Lake Trail near the ~3,300 ft avalanche clearing — it's easy to miss in the trees when descending. Once back on Rachel Lake Trail #1313, it's an easy, well-graded 2+ miles back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required — the summit block's only technical move is a short, low-exposure Class 3 downclimb, not a rappel. Watch the weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in this range and parties often
wa_hibox_mountain_standard.name: Standard Scramble

wa_hozomeen_mountain_north_peak_north_ro.approach: The border gate at Hozomeen has been closed to vehicles and walkers until further notice, so Silver-Skagit Road from Hope, B.C. no longer reaches the trailhead; from the US side Hozomeen is reached by boat up Ross Lake or on the 31-mile East Bank Trail from SR 20. Start at the Hozomeen ranger station, elevation about 1,600 ft, and follow the little Trail of the Obelisk loop. Leave it eastward, cross Howlett Creek, and climb cross-country through moderately open forest on Hozomeen's western flank. There is no trail from here on; the forest is passable on the ascent but reports describe dense brush and jackstraw deadfall as a serious time sink on the way down. Continue to a heathery knoll at about 5,900 ft where you gain the north ridge proper. Round trip is roughly 15 miles with 6,800 ft of gain and the same in loss.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_north_peak_north_ro.descent_text: There are no shortcuts off this mountain and no rappels. Downclimb the northeast ridge, taking the exposed 7,600 ft segment with the same care you gave it on the way up - it is worse in soft afternoon conditions. Descend the north cirque snowfields facing in where they are firm, plunge-stepping or glissaging where they are soft, then regain the north ridge and reverse its several bumps. The real toll is the forest below the 5,900 ft knoll: dense brush and jackstraw deadfall on the west flank made the descent slow enough that one party logged 6.0 hours down against 7.1 hours up, an unusually small gap that tells you how much of the time is spent in the trees. Carry a track; the flank has no distinguishing features and reversing your ascent line matters.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_north_peak_north_ro.name: North Route (North Peak)

wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.approach: There is no US road to Hozomeen. From the Trans-Canada Highway (BC Hwy 1) take Exit 168 at Hope, British Columbia, follow Flood-Hope Road onto Silver-Skagit Road, and drive roughly 34 miles / 55 km of gravel south through Skagit Valley Provincial Park to the Skyline II trailhead — about an hour and a quarter. Verify road and border status first: Silver-Skagit Road has been closed at km 6 for wildfire since 24 July 2026, and NPS has prohibited both vehicle and foot traffic across the boundary at Hozomeen since 2020, with no end date given on the park's fire-closure page updated 14 September 2026. From Skyline II, climb the trail roughly 8 miles and 4,000 ft to the Hozomeen Ridge junction, then turn south on the Hozomeen Ridge Trail over rolling terrain to a camp near the Monument 74 high point at about 6,345 ft, 10.5 miles in. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below Hozomeen Ridge — there is no running water again until you are south of the border. From camp the climb begins by dropping about 545 ft to the 5,800 ft saddle at the head of the north cirque. A shorter but much nastier alternative starts at the Hozomeen ranger station, follows the short Trail of the Obelisk
wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.descent_text: Descend exactly the way you came up. Downclimb the summit blocks and the exposed 7,600 ft step facing inward, taking the same line you climbed — do not try to shortcut the ledge system, because the north cirque side is undercut and the alternatives cliff out. Below the rock, downclimb the upper snowfield facing in, then plunge-step and glissade the lower snowfield to the saddle. Cold, firm morning snow that took crampons cleanly will be soft and rotten on the way down; the same slope that felt secure at 07:00 can be a wet-slide problem at 15:00, and late-season moats at the snow-rock margin are a real trap. Regain the ridge to camp, then reverse the Hozomeen Ridge and Skyline II trails. Parties who camped and descended in one push report roughly six hours from summit back to the trailhead.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.name: Northeast Buttress (North Peak)

wa_hozomeen_mountain_west_face.approach: A two-stage approach and the second stage is the part that stops people. Day one is a long haul of 11-plus miles under heavy loads from the road to a camp just north of the peak - the same Hozomeen Ridge / border-swath ground used by the north-side scrambling routes, reached from Silver-Skagit Road out of Hope, B.C. From that camp the approach to the base took the first ascent party a tedious and painstaking 4.5 hours: downclimb a loose third-class gully, which the party described as dangerous but the lesser of the two evils, then cross several precipitous rocky ribs and steep, unstable ground to traverse into the launch point below the wall. Budget the base approach as a half-day objective in its own right and do it in daylight. Confirm the NPS border-gate status before planning; the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to vehicles and foot traffic since 2020, with no end date given on the park's fire-closure page updated 14 September 2026.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_west_face.descent_text: From the summit, take the easy north-side ground: reverse the Northeast Buttress / North Route line, downclimbing the Class 2-3 northeast ridge, treating the short very exposed Class 4 eroded segment near 7,600 ft with maximum care, then descending the north cirque snowfields to the saddle and back to camp. In late summer, when this route is in condition, those snowfields will be thin or gone, leaving loose rock in their place - carry an axe anyway if any snow remains, and expect the descent to be slower than the grade suggests. Rappelling the west face is not a plan: with almost no protection cracks, every anchor would be a construction project on rotten rock.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_west_face.name: West Face (North Peak)

wa_huckleberry_mountain_east_ridge.approach: From the PCT North Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass (~3,000 ft), hike the PCT northbound via Kendall Pass and the Kendall Katwalk to Ridge Lake, then continue past Alaska Pass and around Joe Lake to the rolling meadows of Huckleberry Flats, roughly 10-11 miles one-way. Most parties camp at Ridge Lake, about 7 miles and 2,700 ft of gain from the trailhead. From Huckleberry Flats, leave the PCT and climb to the base of the east ridge at roughly 6,100 ft, where a rocky buttress marks the start of the technical ridge.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_east_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb back to the notch and rappel off a large pile of rocks with tat on it. A second, lower rappel on the ridge gets you past the 4th-class step and back to easier scrambling terrain leading to the base of the route.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_east_ridge.name: East Ridge

wa_huckleberry_mountain_south_face.approach: Via the Pacific Crest Trail above Joe Lake, then through heather and scree slopes to the base of the south face — the same general approach corridor used for the West Face and East Ridge routes.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_south_face.descent_text: From the summit, either rappel the south face using trees as anchors, or traverse to the East Ridge descent and use its two rappels (off a tat-covered rock pile to the notch, then a second rappel past the 4th-class step) back to the base.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_south_face.name: South Face

wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.approach: Park at the PCT North Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass (I-90 Exit 52, large lot off SR 906/Alpental Rd; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required). Head north on the Pacific Crest Trail; most parties cut the corner via the Commonwealth Basin/Red Pass climbers' shortcut, which rejoins the PCT and trims about a mile off the standard trail. Climb the well-graded PCT switchbacks up to Kendall Katwalk (roughly 5 miles and 2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead) — a dramatic ledge blasted into a cliff face with real exposure in a fall-on-snow scenario early season. Continue north on the PCT past Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, skirting the base of Alaska Mountain, to where the trail runs above Joe Lake, about 10 miles from the pass. For the West Route, leave the trail at a flowery meadow northeast of Joe Lake and head up a talus slope into the basin below the west face, which is clearly visible from there. Alternatively, take the Gold Creek Trail to Joe Lake and hike upslope to the PCT. Water is reliable at Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, and at Joe Lake below the trail. Hazards on the approach include lingering snow on north-facing benches into July, loose rock in the approach gulli
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.descent_text: Rappel the summit block (60m rope recommended) down to the notch, then reverse the gully/ridge down to Huckleberry Flats and rejoin the PCT back to the trailhead; there is no simple walk-off.
wa_huckleberry_mountain_west_route.name: West Face

wa_ingalls_peak_east_ne_ridge_route.approach: From Lake Ingalls, head toward the ridge on climbers' right of the large couloir on the peak's east side; easy ledges lead to the base of the ridge.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_ne_ridge_route.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the East Peak Southwest Face route (3 rap stations) back down to the North-East Peak notch, then reverse the approach terrain to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass.
wa_ingalls_peak_east_ne_ridge_route.name: East Peak (Northeast Ridge to East Face)

wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.approach: Start at the Esmeralda Trailhead (FS Road 9737 end, North Fork Teanaway) and follow the Esmeralda Basin/Lake Ingalls Trail (aka Ingalls Way Trail) north along a rushing creek on an old mining-road grade. At about 0.4 mi a signed junction sends the Longs Pass trail off to the right; stay left/straight for Lake Ingalls. The trail climbs at a moderate, steady grade through Headlight Basin for roughly 3 miles to Ingalls Pass (~6500 ft) and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary — this is the crux navigational/physical checkpoint of the hike-in, gaining close to 2,500-2,800 ft from the trailhead. In early season expect lingering snow and ice on the pass switchbacks; microspikes and an ice axe are worth carrying into July. From Ingalls Pass, drop slightly and traverse boulder-hop terrain into the basin below Lake Ingalls, then climb a large, steep boulder field (hands-and-feet scrambling in spots) to reach Lake Ingalls itself at roughly 4 miles from the trailhead. Lake Ingalls is the last reliable water — filter here before continuing, as there is none higher. From the lake, pick up the climbers' path that skirts the east/right shore and heads up the basin toward the obvious notch between
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.descent_text: The Southwest Face (East Peak's low-fifth-class line) is short — 2 pitches — and the standard descent is to rappel the route itself: three rappel stations are encountered descending the line, using natural anchors (slings around the chockstone/horns typical of this rock, not bolts) rather than fixed hardware. You do not rappel from the summit block itself: parties protect the short scramble down from it to the top station with a handline, and there is a further rappel station down in the approach gully used to regain packs. The first two rappels go on a single rope, but the last is a full double-rope rappel needing two 70 m ropes — a single 60 m rope will not complete this descent, and 70 m ropes are what parties who have done it recommend. Bring an extra sling or two since anchor material on featureless granite here tends to be climber-placed webbing that may need refreshing. The final rappel lands back past the chockstone into the North-East Peak notch/gully, from which you downclimb and scramble the loose gully back down to the basin above Lake Ingalls, retracing the approach. Watch for loose rock in this gully on the way down, especially if other parties are above. As an altern
wa_ingalls_peak_east_route.name: East Peak (Low Fifth Class)

wa_ingalls_peak_friends_in_high_places.approach: From the standard South Ridge/East Ridge approach (Esmeralda trailhead - Longs Pass - Ingalls Pass - above Ingalls Lake), locate the splitter crack system on the slabby southeast face, climber's right of the standard start. Scramble scree to a 3rd/4th-class slab, trending up and rightward to a recessed cave with bolted anchor options at the base of the route.
wa_ingalls_peak_friends_in_high_places.descent_text: The route tops out onto the East Ridge at a large boulder belay after pitch 2; from there, continue up the remaining East Ridge terrain to the summit and descend via the standard South Ridge rappel line (roughly 4 rappels on a 60m rope from the 3-bolt summit anchor).
wa_ingalls_peak_friends_in_high_places.name: Friends In High Places

wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.approach: From the Esmeralda Basin/Ingalls Lake Trailhead (end of Teanaway River Road/USFS Rd 9737), take the Ingalls Way Trail (#1390). At about 0.4 mile bear right at the junction onto Ingalls Way (Esmeralda Basin Trail #1394 continues straight); at roughly 1.4 miles pass the Longs Pass junction. The trail climbs steadily through forest and open slopes to Ingalls Pass (~6,500 ft) at about 3.0-3.1 miles, the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary and your first full view of Mount Stuart and the Ingalls group. From the pass, drop slightly and traverse climbers'-left across open slabs and talus (a boot path braids through here; stay on durable surfaces where possible) for roughly another mile to Lake Ingalls (6,480 ft), about 4-4.5 miles and ~2,500-2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. This is the last reliable water before the climb. From the lake's outlet/left (west) side, scramble up class 2-3 slabs and talus, aiming for the obvious cleft/notch splitting North Ingalls Peak from the main (South) summit, working up to about 7,100 ft. A short section of class 4 leads up a gully to a ledge system at the base of the ridge proper - this is where the roped climbing (pitch 1) begins. No creek fords are i
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the South Ridge climbing line itself (or, for parties who diverge, the closely parallel Southwest Face). From the summit it is four rappels on a single 60 m rope, or three with two 60 m ropes, described here for two ropes: (1) a single-strand rappel down the uppermost pitch to a two-bolt anchor on a narrow ledge; (2) a full-length rappel (double-rope length, i.e. using the rope doubled) down to a large ledge/slung boulder near the top of pitch 2 - do not be tempted to skip straight from the summit to the top of pitch 2 in one long rappel, since a crack just below the top anchor is notorious for wedging and stuck ropes have resulted; breaking it at the pitch-3 ledge avoids this; and (3) a final rappel from that ledge down to the base ledges/gully where the climb started. Anchors are a mix of fixed two-bolt stations and natural slung-boulder/horn anchors reinforced with webbing - carry a few extra feet of tat/webbing since the natural anchors get replaced periodically and can be tired. Below the last rappel, downclimb the class 3-4 gully back to the notch and retrace the approach talus/slabs to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass.
wa_ingalls_peak_south_ridge.name: South Ridge

wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.approach: Start at the West Fork Foss River trailhead (~1,650 ft): from US 2 at Skykomish, turn south on Foss River Road (FR 68), then left on FR 6835 (signed for Trail 1064) for its last 1.9 miles to the trailhead. Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permits are at the trailhead. The West Fork Foss Lakes Trail #1064 reaches Trout Lake at 1.6 miles, then climbs to Copper Lake (4.2 miles, about 2,400 ft of gain) and continues past Little Heart Lake to Big Heart Lake (7.3 miles, about 3,300 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From Big Heart, go cross-country over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past small tarns and Little Chetwoot Lake, to Chetwoot Lake, the usual camp. From Chetwoot, climb talus and heather toward Point 6077, pass it on the east through more talus, and gain Iron Cap's west ridge for easy Class 3 scrambling. A short third-class downclimb drops into a notch; beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, without sidehilling, to the broad north ridge, and easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the 6,347 ft summit. A variation climbs from the Iron Cap Lake outlet on ledges around the nose of the north ridge. Route-finding through the boulder fields is the crux of the appr
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent or loops through the Iron Cap Lake basin. From the summit, follow the broad north ridge down on easy red-tinged rock and dirt, then either return across the ramp and up out of the notch onto the west ridge and down the talus to Chetwoot Lake, or continue down the north ridge to Iron Cap Lake and work back to camp through the lake basin. This is a Class 2-3 walk-off with no fixed anchors or rappels. The main hazards are loose dirt over rock, especially when wet or with snow patches early in the season, and picking the wrong line: parties who lose the ramp or wander east end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands or in steep heather, so retrace your ascent track. From Chetwoot, reverse the cross-country leg over Atrium Ridge to Big Heart Lake and walk the West Fork Foss trail about 7.3 miles back to the trailhead.
wa_iron_cap_mountain_south_route.name: West Ridge / North Ridge via Chetwoot Lake

wa_lane_peak_r1.approach: Same trailhead as the Classic Route: park at the Reflection Lake pullout on Stevens Canyon Road when it's open, or at the Narada Falls pullout in winter/spring when the road is snow-gated (a short, steep ~200 ft climb from Narada Falls regains the road). Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek (~4,500 ft), as with the Classic Route. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face — the Zipper is the obvious left-leaning couloir splitting the center of the face, visible from the road. From the basin, hike up and across a large triangular apron of avalanche/rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloir. From the top of this debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft up the couloir itself to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel/tie-in point. Snow conditions range from styrofoam neve to alpine ice depending on season and aspect; the basin and lower couloir cross avalanche-prone terrain, so this is a start-early, check-the-forecast appr
wa_lane_peak_r1.descent_text: Two descent options are used depending on conditions and whether the party continues to the true summit. Direct reversal (the usual bail line): from the dead-tree notch atop the couloir, downclimb a short stretch of exposed terrain to the tree, which carries fixed rappel slings (a natural, sling-on-tree anchor — not bolted), and make one rappel back down into the Zipper. The rappel is typically just over 100 ft (roughly 30+ m), so it requires a double-rope rappel — two ropes joined, or a single rope doubled — to reach the base cleanly; in a high-snow year a single 70 m rope may just reach, with some downclimbing to finish. From the bottom of the rappel, downclimb/plunge-step the remaining couloir and the debris apron back into the basin and reverse the approach to Tatoosh Creek and the road. Summit-and-walk-off option: instead of rappelling, many parties traverse climber's left from the top of the couloir until the summit slopes come into view and continue to Lane Peak's true summit (a running belay or short pitch on the last 200-300 ft is sometimes prudent), then descend via the standard South Face gully/saddle walk-off shared with the Classic Route (down to the 5,440 ft Lane-Denm
wa_lane_peak_r1.name: The Zipper (couloir)

wa_lane_peak_r2.approach: Same as The Zipper: From Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road (1.5 miles before Snow Lakes Trailhead), hike about 2 miles. Walk briefly along Stevens Canyon Road, then drop into basin toward Tatoosh Creek. Climb up debris triangle and continue to base of couloir system. Identify The Fly as the rightmost/broadest of the three couloirs. Approach takes approximately 45-75 minutes to couloir base.
wa_lane_peak_r2.descent_text: From the top of the Fly at the west-ridge notch, most parties continue around onto the South Face and descend the standard 3rd/4th-class gully route rather than reversing the couloir. Rappelling or downclimbing the Fly itself is also done, particularly by skiers.
wa_lane_peak_r2.name: The Fly (couloir)

wa_lane_peak_r3.approach: Begin at the Narada Falls parking area; travel via snowshoe/ski along the (closed, in winter) Reflection Lakes road, then traverse steep hillsides under Denman Peak toward Lane Peak's base, turning sharply uphill at the first steep avalanche funnel to reach the base of the couloir.
wa_lane_peak_r3.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb to a large tree a few feet below it and rappel from the tree unless the snow is good enough to downclimb. Then plunge-step down moderate slopes toward the Lane–Denman saddle; at the saddle, go to its far left side and descend a steep gully, then retrace the approach. The 100+ ft rappel from the ridge top into the adjacent Zipper couloir (double rope recommended; a 70m rope allows some downclimbing on moderate snow first) is part of the ascent, not the descent.
wa_lane_peak_r3.name: Lover's Lane (couloir)
